title: Built From One Repeated Block
statement: Given a string s, return true if it can be made by writing some shorter block two or more times back to back, and false otherwise.

examples.why: Length 5 is prime, so the only shorter block that could fit is one letter, and the letters differ.
"abaab" twice. The block is not the first run of letters before a repeat ("ab" or "aba"), so guessing from the start fails.

hints: If a block of length d repeats, d must divide the length of s. How many candidate lengths does that leave?
For each divisor d of n with d < n, check whether s[i] === s[i − d] for every i ≥ d. That costs O(n) per divisor, and n has few divisors.
A slicker check: s is periodic exactly when s appears inside (s + s) with the first and last characters removed.

explain.intuition:
If s is a block of length d repeated, then two things hold: d divides n, and every character equals the one d places before it. The second check alone is the definition of "period d". Try every proper divisor of n; there are very few, at most 63 for n ≤ 10 000.

The doubled-string trick says the same thing in one line. Rotating s left by d gives s back exactly when s has period d dividing n. Every rotation of s appears in s + s. Cutting off the first and last character removes the two trivial rotations by 0 and by n, so finding s in what is left means some proper rotation matches.
steps: For each d from 1 to n / 2 where n % d == 0:
Check that s[i] == s[i − d] for all i from d to n − 1. If so, return true.
If no divisor works, return false.
pitfalls: Counting the whole string as its own block. The block must repeat at least twice, so "a" is false.
Guessing the block from the first repeated character. In "abaababaab" the block is "abaab".
Checking a period that does not divide n. "abcabcab" has period 3, but 3 does not divide 8.

complexity.time: O(n · d(n)), where d(n) is the number of divisors

solutions.title: Try every divisor as the block length
solutions.idea: A block length must divide n. For each proper divisor d, check that every character matches the one d positions earlier.

solutions.title: Find s inside the doubled string
solutions.idea: s equals one of its proper rotations exactly when it is a repeated block. All rotations live in s + s; drop the first and last character to exclude the trivial ones.

solutions.title: Prefix function (KMP)
solutions.idea: The longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, L, gives the smallest period p = n − L. The string is a repeated block when L > 0 and p divides n.

followups: Return the shortest block, not just true or false.
Answer the same question for many substrings s[l..r] of one long string. What would you precompute?
